item.text: {"text":"Recent work supports separating history into multiple temporal or intent views. [Beyond Immediate Click (RecSys 2025)](https://doi.org/10.1145/3705328.3748076) describes context-adaptive MoE experts specializing in different time scales, alongside engagement objectives that require signals unavailable here. [MoS (WWW 2026)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.20858) addresses “session hopping”: interests shift between sessions and later recur. Its router extracts theme-consistent subsequences and combines global, short-term and theme-specific experts; authors report fewer FLOPs than competing MoE approaches. [HM4SR (WWW 2025)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.14269) explicitly incorporates timestamp embeddings through temporal experts, but its full multimodal architecture and category-prediction objective exceed the available inputs.\n\nPractical inference for this benchmark: retain a shared SASRec encoder, form inexpensive last-item, short-window, long-history and recent-query attention summaries, then mix their scores using a small gate conditioned on history length, observed log time gaps and disagreement between summaries. This is a proposed adaptation, not an established result from these papers. Include fixed short-only/long-only models, uniform fusion, the existing recent-mean gate and training-popularity controls; remove time gaps and query-dependent retrieval separately. Report macro validation HR@10 plus category and history-length breakdowns, with matched training budgets. Sparse histories remain a specific uncertainty: [ADARec (AAAI 2026)](https://ojs.aaai.org/index.php/AAAI/article/download/38481/42443) uses adaptive diffusion and specialized experts to reconstruct hierarchical intents, but adds substantially more machinery. None of these findings establishes a benefit under the pinned RecHarness evaluation; deletion probes alone cannot establish it either."}
